A soft and welcoming orange glow lights the tunnel, yet the small colony of migrating mollock, that cling to the underside of a stalactites, do not see the 
guiding light, and instead have traveled long following the sweet scent of the slime mold that grows on veins of azacrid. The eight adult bats with their 
three fur-clinging pups could feast on this mold for days before needing to move onwards, and with their goal so close, salivated eagerly. Suddenly a 
short, high pitched squeak resonates off the walls, the echoes reverberating back to the bats, painting the dark tunnel vividly with their echolocating 
senses. Turning back quickly, clicking nervously to better sense the commotion, they witness the last of their group desperately fight off a wet, gripping 
appendage, wrapped around its furred body. Their clicks revealing the sharp glass-like teeth of a false stalactite reeling their kin away from them. The 
ill-fated mollock, knowing there’s now no escape, silences herself, not wanting to call more trouble for her surviving colony. Life in the Umbrawells is swift 
and cruel, and only the hope that her kin will survive without her, will give any solace in her last moments.
Nature will fill any niche, once the sulfur-infused caverns had begun to support a foundation of microbial life, flora and fauna soon 
followed. When certain species fled catastrophes above or explored new opportunities for food below, a new form of life cycle began 
to grow. Scum from the sulfide-based bacteria settled stone and surface water, great colonies of mustermold grew in kind, slowly 
breaking up the hard cold stone of the depths into a kind of deep-soil, akin to the first stirrings of life on the planet's surface billions of 
years earlier. As more fungal species found purchase, a secondary tropic level of small creatures found new homes, worms burrowed, 
arthropods scurried and before long megafauna invaded or evolved to grow large in these sunless lands. 
In the tight labyrinthine confines, many creatures adapted to a crawling, lightless existence. Some relatively recognizable: The mollock 
bat lost its ability to fly, as well as its need to see, and the pallid-scaled krainis snake adapted in a similar way as the use of its thermal 
senses became more than sufficient. Found crawling beneath dark opaque waters or along stalactite strewn ceilings, opportunistic 
skith crustaceans listen intently for the faintest tremor to hunt down and sate their hunger. Though sustenance can be scarce in these 
undergrounds, there is always a stalking predator, and the acrynn fills that role expertly. With wide sonar sensitive antennae on both 
sides of its mandible-filled head, the large, nearly humanoid beetle stalks anything that makes the slightest of sounds.
Flora and Fauna of the Umbrawells
Evolving For A New World
Developing its unique means of navigation 
early, the head of the acrynn grub nearly 
looks like its adult form. Blindly crawling 
along the tunnels its mother left it in, 
quickly eating smaller insects to eventually 
molt into its lithe adult form
With a diet consisting of sulfur eating molds, the beetle's body is 
suffused with enough light producing bacteria to emit a glow of its 
own along long filaments on its abdomen. Lighting the darkness of 
their tunnels to signal to each other when food is found
Round 
and 
less 
sharp-edged 
than its adult forms, the small 
mollucite spends most of its youth 
crawling away from the lair of its 
parents. The young mollusk hoping 
to find  an unused space to let loose 
its thin adhesive tongue to feast on 
the unwary cavern dwellers below
Crawling across the fungal gardens, 
the quills along the beetles abdomen 
brush up against the glowing lanternull, 
collecting and spread the luminescent 
pollen further down the tunnels
Dewmites collect sugary sap from the highly adapted 
subterranean unsundew plant. Instead of converting 
energy from the sun, this plant derives its energy from 
the caustic waters in the loamy fungal soil of the caves
Mounds of pallid quivering flesh-like fungus 
rise off the cavern surfaces. Most of the flora 
and fauna in these dark depths flourishes 
thanks to these unsightly growths, 
filtering the sulfur infused air into 
a cleaner oxygen and mouldering 
into a soil-like layer of sediment
